source_refs.note: Exercise 14.3, Question 9: if a + b + c = 0 then a x b = b x c = c x a (book p.283); condition printed with garbled symbols. Proof, no key answer.

blocks.explanation:
A proof from a given vector equation.
We must show three cross products are equal.
Plan: cross the given equation with \(\underline{a}\), then with \(\underline{b}\), and simplify.
steps:
Given: \(\underline{a} + \underline{b} + \underline{c} = \underline{0}\).
To prove: \(\underline{a} \times \underline{b} = \underline{b} \times \underline{c} = \underline{c} \times \underline{a}\).
Method: Crossing both sides of an equation with the same vector keeps it true. Then use \(\underline{x} \times \underline{x} = \underline{0}\), \(\underline{x} \times \underline{0} = \underline{0}\), the distributive law and \(\underline{x} \times \underline{y} = -\underline{y} \times \underline{x}\).

Cross with \(\underline{a}\) on the left
\[\underline{a} \times (\underline{a} + \underline{b} + \underline{c}) = \underline{a} \times \underline{0}\]
\[\underline{a} \times \underline{a} + \underline{a} \times \underline{b} + \underline{a} \times \underline{c} = \underline{0}\]
\[\underline{0} + \underline{a} \times \underline{b} - \underline{c} \times \underline{a} = \underline{0}\]
\[\underline{a} \times \underline{b} = \underline{c} \times \underline{a} \quad (1)\]
Why: Distributive law; \(\underline{a} \times \underline{a} = \underline{0}\) (angle 0) and \(\underline{a} \times \underline{c} = -\underline{c} \times \underline{a}\).

Cross with \(\underline{b}\) on the left
\[\underline{b} \times (\underline{a} + \underline{b} + \underline{c}) = \underline{b} \times \underline{0}\]
\[\underline{b} \times \underline{a} + \underline{b} \times \underline{b} + \underline{b} \times \underline{c} = \underline{0}\]
\[-\underline{a} \times \underline{b} + \underline{0} + \underline{b} \times \underline{c} = \underline{0}\]
\[\underline{a} \times \underline{b} = \underline{b} \times \underline{c} \quad (2)\]
Why: Same rules: \(\underline{b} \times \underline{b} = \underline{0}\), \(\underline{b} \times \underline{a} = -\underline{a} \times \underline{b}\).

Combine (1) and (2)
\[\underline{a} \times \underline{b} = \underline{b} \times \underline{c} = \underline{c} \times \underline{a}\]
Why: Both \(\underline{b} \times \underline{c}\) and \(\underline{c} \times \underline{a}\) equal \(\underline{a} \times \underline{b}\).

Check with an example
\[\underline{a} = \underline{i},\ \underline{b} = \underline{j},\ \underline{c} = -\underline{i} - \underline{j}\]
\[\underline{a} \times \underline{b} = \underline{k}\]
\[\underline{b} \times \underline{c} = -\underline{j} \times \underline{i} = \underline{k}\]
\[\underline{c} \times \underline{a} = -\underline{j} \times \underline{i} = \underline{k}\]
Why: \(\underline{a} + \underline{b} + \underline{c} = \underline{0}\) here and all three products are \(\underline{k}\).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The condition of Question 9 is printed with garbled symbols (the vector \(\underline{c}\) and the plus signs are broken). The intended condition is \(\underline{a} + \underline{b} + \underline{c} = \underline{0}\).
